title: The Coming of the Third Reich
author: Richard J. Evans

title: Grid Systems
author: Josef Müller-Brockmann
verdict: The classic. Still the clearest explanation of why grids work.
review: Müller-Brockmann explains the grid as a way of thinking, not a template. The worked examples make the reasoning easy to follow.
Dense in places, but every page earns its spot. It sits on the desk rather than the shelf.

title: Ikigai
author: Héctor García & Francesc Miralles
verdict: Pleasant and calming, though lighter than its reputation.
review: Built around interviews in Okinawa, it is more a collection of gentle observations than a method. Some sections feel padded.
Worth it for the idea of staying busy with purpose, and it is a quick read.

title: Atomic Habits
author: James Clear
verdict: Small, almost boring changes, stacked until they compound.
review: The core idea fits on a sticky note: make good habits obvious and easy, make bad ones invisible and awkward. What makes the book useful is how practical it gets about the environment around a habit rather than willpower.
It repeats itself in the second half, but the chapters on habit stacking and identity are worth coming back to.

title: Factfulness
author: Hans Rosling
verdict: A calm, data-led argument that the world is better than our instincts say.
review: Rosling opens with a quiz most experts fail, then works through the ten instincts that skew how we read the news. It is warm and funny rather than smug.
The charts are the star. It changed how I read headlines with big numbers in them.

title: The Psychology of Money
author: Morgan Housel
verdict: Less about money than about behaviour, luck and patience.
review: Short chapters, each built around a story. The point is that how you behave with money matters more than how clever you are with it.
Easy to read in a weekend and easy to lend to someone who would never pick up a finance book.

title: Newspaper Design
author: Javier Errea (ed.)
verdict: A rich survey of how great newsrooms design for print.
review: Case studies from papers around the world, with plenty of spreads to study. The essays on structure and hierarchy translate directly to digital work.
A book to dip into for reference rather than read cover to cover.

title: Warrior Saints
author: Amandeep Singh Madra & Parmjit Singh
bestFor: A slow read at the weekend
verdict: A beautifully made book that treats its subject with real care.
review: The archive photography carries a lot of this book. Each portrait gets room to breathe, and the captions add context without crowding the images.
Still working through it a chapter at a time.
